topic.title: Polar Function Graphs
topic.summary: Graphing r = f(θ) in polar coordinates: reading angle as direction and output as signed radius, connecting the rectangular graph of r against θ to the polar curve, and restricting the domain to draw part of a curve.

lesson.title: Polar Function Graphs
lesson.summary: Graphing r = f(θ) in polar coordinates: reading angle as direction and output as signed radius, connecting the rectangular graph of r against θ to the polar curve, and restricting the domain to draw part of a curve.
lesson.bigIdea: A polar function turns each angle into a distance. Sweep θ around the origin and move out (or back) by r = f(θ): circles, cardioids, and roses all come from that one rule.
lesson.context: Topic 3.13 plotted single points (r, θ). Here r depends on θ, so the points form a curve. The rectangular graph of r against θ is the best tool for predicting the polar picture.

sections.title: 3.14.A · Input is an angle; output is a signed radius.

blocks.text: The graph of the function r = f(θ) in polar coordinates consists of input-output pairs of values where the input values are angle measures and the output values are radii.

When graphing polar functions in the form of r = f(θ), changes in input values relate to changes in angle measures from the polar axis, and changes in output values relate to changes in signed radial displacements from the origin.

blocks.caption: r = 2 + 2 cos θ graphed with θ on the horizontal axis
blocks.alt: A cosine-shaped wave from r = 4 at θ = 0 down to r = 0 at θ = π and back up to r = 4 at θ = 2π.

blocks.caption: The same function in polar coordinates. Move the slider to trace the curve from θ = 0.
blocks.alt: A heart-shaped curve called a cardioid on a polar grid. It starts 4 units out on the polar axis, passes 2 units up the positive y-axis, reaches the origin at θ = π, and returns symmetrically below the axis.

blocks.text: Reading the two graphs together: as θ increases from 0 to π, r decreases from 4 to 0, so the curve sweeps counterclockwise while moving in toward the origin. From π to 2π, r increases back to 4.

blocks.caption: Common polar graphs
rows: Circle of radius 3 centered at the origin
Limaçon with an inner loop where r < 0

sections.takeaway: Sweep the angle, set the signed distance, and use the r–θ graph to predict the shape.

sections.title: 3.14.A · Restrict the domain to draw part of a polar graph.
sections.conceptTitle: Restricting the domain and negative radii

blocks.text: The domain of the polar function r = f(θ), given graphically, can be restricted to a desired portion of the function by selecting endpoints corresponding to the desired angle and radius.

blocks.caption: r = 3 sin(2θ): the whole rose (dashed) and the petal drawn by 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2
blocks.alt: A four-petal rose on a polar grid, drawn dashed, with one petal in Quadrant I drawn solid. The solid petal starts and ends at the origin and reaches 3 units out at θ = π/4.

blocks.text: For r = 3 sin(2θ), r = 0 at θ = 0 and θ = π/2 and r = 3 at θ = π/4, so 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 draws exactly the petal in Quadrant I. On π/2 < θ < π, sin(2θ) < 0, so r < 0 and those points land in the opposite quadrant, Quadrant IV.

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: For π/2 < θ < π, r = 3 sin(2θ) is negative, so the points of the graph are in Quadrant IV, opposite the terminal rays of θ in Quadrant II.

sections.takeaway: Pick θ-endpoints where r = 0 (or at the desired radius) to isolate a piece; negative r reflects through the origin.

vocabulary.definition: The graph of the function r = f(θ) in polar coordinates consists of input-output pairs of values where the input values are angle measures and the output values are radii.

connections.title: Plotting polar points
connections.body: Topic 3.13 placed points with negative r on the opposite side of the origin. A polar graph is many such points, so the same rule explains loops and petals.
connections.transferQuestion: For r = 1 + 2 cos θ, find r at θ = π and say where the point is.
connections.feedback: r = 1 − 2 = −1, so the point is 1 unit along the ray opposite π, at (1, 0) in rectangular coordinates.

connections.title: Moving toward or away from the origin
connections.body: Topic 3.15 uses the sign of r and whether r is increasing or decreasing to tell when the curve moves away from the origin, and it measures the average rate of change of r with respect to θ.
connections.transferQuestion: On 0 < θ < π, is the cardioid r = 2 + 2 cos θ moving toward or away from the origin?
connections.feedback: Toward: r is positive and decreasing.

glossary.definition: The polar coordinate system is based on a grid of circles centered at the origin and on lines through the origin. The positive x-axis is called the polar axis. Polar coordinates of a point are defined as an ordered pair, (r, θ). The value of θ is given by the measure of an angle in standard position whose terminal ray lies in a line that passes through the point, and r is the radial displacement of the point from the origin.
The positive x-axis is called the polar axis.
The graph of the function r = f(θ) in polar coordinates consists of input-output pairs of values where the input values are angle measures and the output values are radii.
